studies.title: Sent Down On A Blessed Night
studies.meaning: An oath by the clear Book, and then a claim about timing: We sent it down on a blessed night. Which night has been read in more than one way. One reading identifies it with the night of decree named elsewhere in the Quran, in the month the Quran says the revelation began; another places it in the middle of an earlier month, and the classical commentaries record both. The next line says that in it every wise matter is separated out, read either as the year's affairs being distinguished or as this revelation being set apart, again without a settled decision.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, opening a short surah named for a smoke described a few lines later. The audience knew what a night of decision meant from their own practice of settling matters for the season. Commentators note that the surah spends its opening on where the revelation came from before it says anything about what it contains. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: From a root for something settling and remaining, used of water gathering in a pool. A blessed thing in this vocabulary is one that stays and increases rather than one merely approved.
A passive verb for dividing one thing from another, from the root behind the word for a criterion. It occurs only here in this form, and it names sorting rather than deciding.
The adjective is attached to the matter rather than to a person, which readers of Arabic have long noticed. It carries both wisdom and the sense of something made firm.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian communities had nights of decision of their own. Before a season's migration or a major expedition, elders met and settled what would be done, and the arrangements held until the next such meeting. Everyone understood a fixed point in the year when matters that had been open were closed. The vocabulary of separating out belonged to that practice before it was applied here.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for a blessed night occurs only in this ayah, and the passive verb for matters being separated out occurs only in the line that follows it. Two consecutive ayat contain two expressions the Quran never uses again, which is part of why the classical commentators discuss this passage at such length.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage attaches revelation to a moment rather than presenting it as timeless, which gives the text a beginning inside history. It also introduces a picture of matters being sorted rather than invented, so what descends is described as distinguished from a larger whole already held. That the identification of the night is left open is itself instructive: the Quran names a time without fixing it, and the tradition has carried the range rather than closing it.

crossReferences.why: Names a night of decree better than a thousand months, on which the angels and the Spirit descend.
Names the month in which the Quran was sent down, as guidance for people and clear proofs.
Uses the same root for a criterion given to those mindful of God, separating one thing from another.

studies.applyIt: Pick one night this month and decide in advance to stay awake for an extra half hour with the Quran, not because that night is the one but because you will never establish which it is. This passage names a night and leaves it unidentified, and the practical response to that is more nights, not fewer.

studies.title: A Mercy From Your Lord
studies.meaning: The sentence that began with the sending continues: it was a mercy from your Lord. Commentators note that revelation is classified here rather than described, and the classification is not information or warning but mercy. Then names accumulate. He hears and He knows; He is Lord of the heavens and the earth and what lies between, if you would be certain; there is no god but He, and He gives life and death. The last line lands hard after all that. Yet they are in doubt, playing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following the surah's opening statement about a blessed night. The chain of statements about God's lordship answers an audience who already accepted a creator while behaving otherwise. Commentators note that the phrase about the Lord of your forefathers of old cuts across the appeal to ancestors that the surrounding surahs record repeatedly. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: The word's root is the one behind the term for a womb. Naming the revelation as mercy places it in that register of protection and provision rather than in the register of instruction.
From a root for knowledge that has settled and stopped moving. The condition attached to the previous statement asks not for belief but for the kind of knowing that no longer wavers.
The plain verb for play, put in a form describing something ongoing. Doubt is not presented here as a serious position but as an activity people are passing the time with.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccans swore by their ancestors constantly and traced authority through them, which made the phrase about the Lord of their forefathers a claim on ground they thought was theirs. The same God is being named as the one those ancestors also stood under. In a society where an argument was usually won by producing an older precedent, that move took the precedent and kept it.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah names God as Lord of the heavens and the earth and what lies between them, a formula the Quran uses repeatedly to leave no region unnamed. Within four ayat here it moves from a mercy to a hearing and knowing to a lordship over everything to the giving of life and death, and then ends on a single word for play.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage classifies revelation as mercy before saying anything about its content, which sets the terms for everything after. A warning delivered as mercy is a different object from a warning delivered as a threat, even where the words are identical. And the closing line makes an assessment of doubt worth noticing: not that these people have examined the matter and remain unconvinced, but that they have not treated it as serious.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same classification for the Prophet's whole mission, calling him a mercy to all the worlds.
Describes the revelation as healing and mercy for the believers, adding what it does to those who take it.
Shows Abraham refusing his forefathers' objects of worship, the argument this passage's phrasing turns around.

studies.applyIt: Take one passage of the Quran that reads to you as a threat and reread it holding this ayah's classification in mind, that the whole thing came as mercy. Do not force a warm feeling. Just notice whether reading a warning as protection rather than as an attack changes anything about how the words sit.

studies.title: A Smoke Covering The People
studies.meaning: The Prophet is told to watch for a day when the sky brings a visible smoke that covers people, and their cry is quoted: our Lord, remove the punishment from us, we are believers. Commentators divide over what the smoke is, some taking it as a severe famine already experienced in Mecca and others as a sign still to come, and the classical sources carry both. The passage then answers the promise itself. How can a reminder reach them now, when a clear messenger already came and they turned away calling him taught and possessed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The commentators record a severe drought in Mecca during the years of opposition, in which hunger was said to make people see a haze in the air, and some read the smoke against that. Others place it among the signs preceding the Hour. Both readings are transmitted. The two words thrown at the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) in the last line are recorded as actual Meccan accusations.

keyTerms.note: A verb for keeping a lookout from a height, used of a sentry. It appears here and again in the surah's final ayah, so the whole chapter sits between two instructions to watch.
A verb for enveloping something so it is hidden, used of night falling. It describes the smoke as a covering rather than as a burning, which is why the picture is oppressive rather than violent.
A passive participle, so the charge is that he received his material from a teacher. Paired with the second accusation, it makes two incompatible claims in a single breath.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Famine in Arabia had a look. Dust hung in the still air over a dry season, the horizon went pale, and people spoke of a haze that would not lift. Hunger itself was said to affect the eyes. Whether or not that is what this ayah names, the description would have matched something the audience had seen, which is why the reading persisted.
studies.didYouKnow: The instruction to watch out that opens this passage appears again as the final word of the surah's last ayah, so the chapter is framed by the same verb at both ends. The word for smoke that gives the surah its name occurs here, and once more in the Quran describing the heaven before it was formed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage records a promise of belief made under pressure and treats it as worth nothing, which is a hard judgement and a consistent one. What is being tested is not whether people can be brought to say the right words but whether anything remains once the pressure lifts. It also notes the shape of the original refusal: two accusations that cancel each other, taught and mad, offered together by people who were not weighing either.

crossReferences.why: Completes the judgement, saying the punishment will be lifted a little and they will go back to it.
Describes the same pattern, mercy shown and harm removed while they persist in wandering blindly.
Records a promise made at the sight of the Fire, and says they would return to what they were forbidden.

studies.applyIt: Recall the last time you made a serious promise while frightened: in a waiting room, before a result, during turbulence. Ask what happened to it. Do not resolve to do better under pressure. Instead, make one small commitment now, while nothing is wrong, and see whether it survives a month.

studies.title: Hand Over God's Servants
studies.meaning: The relief is announced and undercut in one breath: We are lifting the punishment a little, and you will go back. Then a day of the great seizing is named. The surah turns to a precedent, and the demand Moses brings is stated in unexpected terms. Hand over to me the servants of God, and I am to you a trustworthy messenger. Commentators read the demand as the release of the enslaved Israelites, and note that they are called God's servants in the same sentence in which they are being claimed from a man who considered them his.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah addressing a community under pressure from a power that would not yield. The account of Pharaoh is used across the Meccan surahs as the standing example of what such power does and how it ends. Commentators report no occasion for these ayat. Slavery and the transfer of dependent people between owners were familiar in Arabia, which is why the demand's phrasing lands as it does.

keyTerms.note: A noun for grabbing with violent force, joined to the superlative for greatest. The phrase occurs only here, and it names an action rather than a place or a period.
The verb used for returning a trust or paying a debt. Applying it to people asks for their release as the settling of an obligation rather than as a favour.
From the root behind faith and security, describing someone with whom something can safely be left. It was also the title the Meccans themselves used for the Prophet before his mission.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Trusts were the backbone of Arabian commerce. Goods, money and people were left in another man's keeping while their owner travelled, and the whole system ran on the reputation of those who could be trusted to return what was left. The verb Moses uses is that verb, which frames the enslaved as a deposit held by someone who is being asked to give it back.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for the greatest seizing occurs only in this ayah. The word Moses uses of himself, trustworthy, is the same one the Meccans had used as a byname for the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) before he began to preach, and the Quran gives it to several messengers as their self-description in almost identical wording.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names the enslaved as servants of God while they are still in another man's possession, which settles the question of ownership before the negotiation begins. It also shows relief being given as part of a judgement rather than as its reversal. The pause is described in advance as temporary, and the accuracy of that description is what makes the passage uncomfortable rather than reassuring.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same demand in nearly the same words, telling Pharaoh to send the Children of Israel with them.
Has Moses describe himself as a messenger from the Lord of the worlds and ask for the same release.
Gives the identical self-description, a trustworthy messenger, in the mouth of an earlier prophet.

studies.applyIt: Think of something in your keeping that is not yours: borrowed money, a lent book, an obligation you took on. Return one of them this week without being asked. The verb in this ayah is the ordinary verb for giving back a trust, and using it about human beings only works because everyone already knew what it demanded.

studies.title: I Have Taken Refuge
studies.meaning: Three requests and then a withdrawal. Do not exalt yourselves above God; I come with clear authority; I have taken refuge in my Lord and your Lord against your stoning me. And if you do not believe me, then leave me alone. Commentators note the last one especially: not a threat and not a plea, simply a request for separation. Only after that does he turn away and call on his Lord. The instruction that comes back is practical rather than triumphant. Travel by night with My servants, because you will be pursued.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Stoning was a real method of dealing with someone whose presence had become intolerable, used across the region, and the Quran records other prophets being threatened with it. Commentators read the sequence as a mission running out of options step by step. The believers in Mecca at this time were also in the position of asking to be left alone. No specific occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A verb for physical height, used of exalting oneself. The word describes the posture rather than any particular act, which is how the Quran characterises this ruler throughout.
The past tense: the refuge is already taken, not being requested. The word occurs twice in the Quran, both times spoken by someone facing a threat from this same court.
A verb for withdrawing to one side. He asks for distance rather than for acceptance, which is a request a person makes when the argument itself has been given up on.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Leaving by night was how vulnerable groups moved. Caravans travelled in darkness to avoid heat and to avoid being seen, and anyone escaping a stronger party did the same. The instruction here is not miraculous but tactical, the ordinary advice anyone in the region would have given, and its plainness is part of what makes the account feel close to the ground.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact form of the verb for taking refuge that Moses uses occurs twice in the Quran, and both occurrences are spoken in the presence of the same ruler, once by Moses himself and once by a believing man of the court who concealed his faith. The word is rare and its two uses belong to the same story.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage shows a prophet asking to be left alone, which the Quran records without embarrassment. Withdrawal after a message has been delivered is presented as a legitimate step rather than a failure. It also separates refuge from rescue. He states that he has already taken refuge while the danger is still present and unresolved, so the refuge is not described as an outcome but as a position taken.

crossReferences.why: Gives the only other use of this word for refuge, spoken at the same court by a man concealing his faith.
Shows Abraham threatened with stoning by his father and withdrawing from him with a greeting.
Repeats the instruction to travel by night with the servants and to strike a dry path through the sea.

studies.applyIt: Identify one conversation you keep re-entering that has never once moved. Say your position clearly one final time, then ask for distance and take it. This ayah has a prophet requesting to be left alone, which means the request is not weakness. It is what comes after the argument has been honestly made.

studies.title: How Much They Left Behind
studies.meaning: An instruction about the sea, and then an inventory. Leave the sea parted and still; they are an army to be drowned. How many gardens and springs they left, and cultivated fields, and a noble station, and a comfort they used to take pleasure in. Commentators note the list is not of what was destroyed but of what was abandoned, still standing and no longer theirs. The passage closes flatly. So it was, and We made another people inherit it, with nothing said about who or whether they deserved it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Egypt's irrigated wealth was known to Arabian traders as the region's most conspicuous prosperity, which makes the inventory pointed for an audience whose own leading families were being addressed. Commentators note that the surah has already listed the ornaments of comfortable people in an earlier passage of this period. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: A word for something calm and left as it is, occurring only here. Commentators read it as leaving the sea open and quiet rather than closing it, which is what makes the pursuit possible.
A place where one stands, joined to the adjective for generous and honourable. It covers both a fine dwelling and a position of standing, and the ambiguity is not resolved.
From the root for fruit, describing people enjoying themselves the way one enjoys sweet things. It names pleasure taken lightly rather than possessions held.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Egypt was the granary of the region. Its canals, orchards and stone buildings were spoken of by traders who had seen them, and Arabian audiences had a clear picture of a wealth their own land could not produce. Listing gardens, springs and standing crops named exactly the things a person from the Hijaz would have found most impressive and least imaginable at home.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the sea left still and parted occurs only in this ayah, and the word for those taking their ease appears twice in the Quran, once here for a people about to be drowned and once for those at rest in the Garden. The same word covers both kinds of comfort, and only the ending differs.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates possessions from their owners without destroying either. The gardens remain; the people do not. That is a different and quieter claim than one about wealth being punished, and it puts the emphasis on transfer rather than on loss. The final line then refuses to say anything about the inheritors, which leaves the reader without the consolation of a moral about who deserves what.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same inventory of what was left, and says We made the Children of Israel inherit it.
Names the inheritance of the eastern and western parts of the land, blessed for a people long oppressed.
Describes towns whose dwellings were not inhabited after them, and says We were the inheritors.

studies.applyIt: Walk through one room of your home and pick out three things you would not have thought to list if someone asked what you own. Then imagine the room described by somebody after you, in a sentence beginning with how much they left. The inventory in this ayah is short, and it is complete.

studies.title: The Sky Did Not Weep
studies.meaning: One of the strangest sentences in the Quran: neither the heaven nor the earth wept over them, and they were not given respite. Commentators note that the denial implies the possibility. Something can be wept for by the sky and the ground, and these were not. Then the deliverance is stated from the other side, the Children of Israel taken out of a humiliating punishment, and the man responsible named as high-handed and excessive. The passage ends by saying they were chosen knowingly and given signs containing a clear test, which is not the same as a reward.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The account of Pharaoh's end is used throughout the Meccan surahs as reassurance for a community with no visible prospect of relief. Commentators note the closing lines refuse to let deliverance be read as a permanent guarantee, since what follows the rescue is described as a test. No specific occasion is reported. The image of the sky weeping was familiar from Arabic elegy for the dead.

keyTerms.note: The plain verb for weeping, occurring in this form only here. Denying it of the sky and the earth assumes a world in which those things can mourn, and reports that they did not.
The active participle of rising above, the same root as the warning Moses delivered to him earlier in the surah. He is described by the very thing he had been told not to do.
A word covering both a favour bestowed and an affliction sent, since either can be a test. Attached to signs given after a rescue, it holds both senses at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabic elegy said that the sky wept for a great man, that the stars dimmed and the wind mourned. It was a fixed poetic move, and audiences knew it as the highest form of tribute a poet could pay. Saying flatly that neither the heaven nor the earth wept for these people used that convention by withholding it, which every listener would have felt.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for weeping appears in this form only in this ayah, in a sentence denying that it happened. Arabic elegy conventionally claimed the sky wept for the dead, so the Quran's single use of the word takes a stock poetic tribute and reports its absence, without ever describing what a mourned death would have looked like.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage measures a life by what its ending occasions rather than by what it accumulated. Nothing is said about punishment here; what is recorded is that nothing marked the loss. Then the deliverance of the other party is immediately qualified as a test, which keeps rescue from becoming status. Being chosen is described as coming with signs attached, and signs are things a people can fail.

crossReferences.why: States the same favour given to the Children of Israel, the Book and the judgement and good provisions.
Has Moses tell them their Lord may make them successors and then see how they act, framing rescue as a test.
Asks whether any of the earlier generations can be sensed or heard now, in the same register of absence.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone whose death would leave a real gap in a place, not only in people: a shop, a mosque row, a street. Then ask, without answering too quickly, what would be different where you are if you were not there. This ayah measures a life by what its absence changes, and the measure is worth borrowing.

studies.title: Not Created In Play
studies.meaning: An objection is quoted and then answered from two directions. The objection sets its own terms for proof: bring back our ancestors. The first answer is historical and points at a kingdom stronger than theirs that is no longer there. The second is structural and much larger. The heavens and the earth were not made in play. The commentators read that word precisely, since it names activity with no purpose beyond its own performance, so the argument is that a pointless universe is the assumption hidden inside the denial.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The people named here were the Himyarite kingdom of south Arabia, whose rulers carried that title, and their cities and inscriptions were known to Arabian traders. Naming them rather than a distant empire put the argument within reach of the objectors, who could ask their own caravans about the place. The Quran mentions them in only one other passage, in a similar list.

keyTerms.note: From a verb meaning to unfold or spread something that was rolled, used of opening a scroll. Resurrection is pictured as a thing unfurled rather than reassembled from parts.
Not a personal name but the title borne by rulers of a south Arabian kingdom, in the way other peoples are named here by their king. The Quran uses it in only two places.
Activity with no purpose beyond its own doing. The word is not dismissive of games; it names the absence of an end outside the act, which is exactly the claim being denied.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The winter caravan went south to Yemen, and the road passed the remains of the old south Arabian kingdoms: the great broken dam, terraced fields gone dry, inscriptions in a script Meccans could see and not read. Merchants dealt with the region every year and knew its history as commercial knowledge rather than legend. A reference to that people pointed at something the audience had walked past.
studies.didYouKnow: The people named in this passage appear in only one other place in the whole Quran, again in a list of earlier communities that rejected their messengers. The Quran identifies them by a royal title rather than by a personal or tribal name, which is in fact how the rulers of that south Arabian kingdom were designated in their own inscriptions.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument runs from purpose rather than from power. Instead of asserting that God is able to raise the dead, the passage asks what kind of world the denial requires, and names it as play. That reverses the direction of the question: a reckoning is presented as the thing that makes the whole arrangement coherent rather than as an extra claim added on top of it. The next ayah states the same point positively.

crossReferences.why: Contains the only other mention of the same people, again among those who denied their messengers.
States the same denial about the heavens and the earth, and adds what would follow had it been otherwise.
Puts the argument as a direct question about the reader: did you suppose you were created for nothing?

studies.applyIt: Spend five minutes writing what you would do differently tomorrow if you were certain the arrangement had a purpose. Then look at your list and mark the items you could do anyway, regardless of what you are certain of. Most people find the list barely changes. That gap is what this passage is actually about.

studies.title: The Day Of Sorting Out
studies.meaning: Creation is stated to have a purpose and most people are said not to know it. Then the appointment: the day of separation is the fixed time for all of them together. Commentators note that the word for a fixed time is the ordinary word for an appointment, so the scene is administrative rather than dramatic. The next line withdraws the one thing everybody counts on. No ally will avail an ally in anything, and they will not be helped. Then one exception, and it is not a category of person but an act: except whoever God has mercy on.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, following a statement that the heavens and the earth were not created in play. The audience's social world ran entirely on alliance, so the withdrawal of a patron's usefulness on that Day named the thing they were most confident of. Commentators report no occasion. The sequence moves from purpose in creation to a fixed appointment to the dissolution of every arrangement people had made under it.

keyTerms.note: From the verb for cutting one thing away from another, the same root used at the surah's opening for matters being separated out. The Day is named by an act of sorting.
The ordinary word for a fixed appointment, used elsewhere of the time and place set for pilgrimage. It makes the Day an entry in a schedule rather than an interruption of one.
The word covers a patron, a client, a freed slave's former owner and a cousin. It is used twice in one clause, so both parties to any such bond are named at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every person in Mecca could name their allies. The bond covered blood money, protection on the road, standing in a dispute and burial, and it ran in both directions between unequal parties. It was the single most reliable thing in a person's life. Naming it twice in one clause and then cancelling it removed the entire framework the audience used to think about safety.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for an ally appears twice within the same short clause, once for each side of the relationship, so the sentence cancels the bond from both directions at once. The name given to the Day comes from the same root as the verb in the surah's fourth ayah, where every wise matter is described as being separated out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage removes every intermediary and then reintroduces one thing, mercy, which is not something anyone can be allied to. That distinction matters. An ally can be cultivated, obliged and called upon; mercy cannot be arranged in advance, and the sentence deliberately gives it as a verb rather than as a status. What is left is a direct relation with no one standing in between.

crossReferences.why: Denies that any soul will avail another, or that intercession or compensation will be accepted for it.
Says no father will avail his child and no child his father, naming the closest bond of all.
Uses the same name for the Day, calling it an appointed time when the trumpet is blown and people come.

studies.applyIt: Write down the three people you would call first in a genuine emergency. Look at the list and say a short prayer for each of them by name. This ayah says such bonds will not help on that Day, which is not a reason to hold them loosely now, but it is a reason to ask for something better for them than help.

studies.title: A Tree That Feeds The Sinner
studies.meaning: A tree is named and given a function: it is the food of the persistent sinner. Then two comparisons, one after the other, both about heat. Like molten metal boiling in the bellies, like the boiling of scalding water. Commentators note that the passage describes a substance by what it does rather than by what it looks like. Then the register changes entirely into a command shouted to unnamed agents: seize him and drag him to the middle of the blaze. The scene arrives with no transition, and the shift is the point.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The tree named here appears in another Meccan surah where the Quran records the objection that a tree could not grow in the Fire, and commentators report that this image in particular was mocked. The audience were people for whom molten metal was a workshop reality. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat, which belong to the surah's contrast between two outcomes.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form from the root for sin, describing someone characterised by it rather than someone who has done it. The definite article narrows the description further.
A word for metal melted down or the sediment of oil, thick and scalding. The Quran uses it three times, always for something that scalds by pouring rather than by burning.
A verb for hauling someone roughly by force, occurring only here. The imperative is plural and its addressees are never named, which is part of what makes the line land.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Metalworking was familiar in Arabian towns. Smiths melted down silver and copper, and everyone had seen the surface of molten metal and knew what a splash of it did. The comparison is not exotic; it names something people had watched a craftsman handle carefully with tongs. The second comparison, to boiling water, brings the same heat into the kitchen.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for dragging someone off occurs only in this ayah in the Quran. The tree's name appears three times, and in one of them it sits inside a question asking whether that tree or a welcome laid out for guests is the better hospitality, so the same tree is set against a host's table in one surah and served as food in this one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage describes consequence in physical terms and then hands the scene over to voices without identifying them, which produces something closer to overhearing than to being told. That method leaves the reader inside the scene rather than in front of it. Placing this immediately before the description of the secure is also deliberate: the surah keeps both possibilities available at once and refuses to let either be read alone.

crossReferences.why: Names the same tree, calls it a trial for the wrongdoers, and contrasts it with a welcome laid out.
Uses the same word for molten dregs, describing water given to those who ask for relief.
Gives the answering half of the contrast, the God-conscious in a secure station among gardens and springs.

studies.applyIt: Read this passage once and then read the four ayat that follow it, without stopping between them. Notice what happens in your chest at the change. The surah does not let the first scene stand alone, and reading it alone is a choice the text does not make for you.

studies.title: Taste It You Mighty One
studies.meaning: The command continues: then pour over his head the punishment of scalding water. Then a line of pure irony. Taste, you who are the mighty, the noble. Commentators note that the two words are titles the man had held or claimed, returned to him at the moment they mean nothing. The next line names what the whole scene answers: this is the thing you kept doubting. Then, without transition, the surah turns. The God-conscious are in a secure station, among gardens and springs, and the word for their place is the word for safety.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The two titles used ironically here were live currency in Mecca, where standing was described in exactly these terms and men were addressed by them in the assembly. Commentators note that the Quran uses the same two words elsewhere as descriptions of God and of the revelation. No specific occasion is reported. The turn to the God-conscious closes the surah's paired outcomes.

keyTerms.note: Water heated to its limit. The same word in Arabic can also mean a close friend, which is a coincidence of roots the classical commentators note without building anything on it.
Two words of honour, used here with the opposite of their meaning. Both appear elsewhere in the Quran as genuine descriptions, which is what gives their misuse here its edge.
A place of standing joined to the adjective for safe and trustworthy. The security is attached to the location itself rather than to any guard set over it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Titles were used constantly and mattered enormously. A man was addressed by the honorific his standing earned him, and being denied one in public was a recognisable insult. Sarcasm delivered by using someone's own title back at him was a known and cutting move in the assemblies, well understood by everyone present. The line in this ayah is that move.
studies.didYouKnow: The two words of honour used sarcastically here appear together elsewhere in the Quran as genuine attributes, one of them among the names of God and both of them describing the revelation. This is the only place where the pair is applied to a human being, and it is applied to him at the moment nothing about him is either.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates the reversal in language rather than in force. The punishment is described briefly; the title returned to the man is what does the work. That says something about what standing actually consists of, since it can be dissolved simply by being repeated at the wrong moment. And the immediate turn to the secure station makes safety, not honour, the thing the surah presents as worth having.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same scalding water and shade, for people who had lived in ease before that.
Turns from a punishment scene to the sincere servants in the same abrupt way, with honour named as theirs.
Records the doubt that this scene answers, their claim that there is only the first death and no raising.

studies.applyIt: Think of a title you like being given: a job description, a role in a family, a reputation among friends. Say it to yourself once, plainly, and ask what would remain of you if it were removed tomorrow. This ayah returns a man his titles at the one moment they hold nothing, and the exercise costs nothing to try early.

studies.title: Facing One Another
studies.meaning: The description is short and every element is social. They wear fine silk and heavy brocade, facing one another, which commentators read as seated so that nobody has their back to anyone. Companions are given, fruit is called for and comes, and the whole is described as being in security. Then the last line does something the others do not. They will not taste death there beyond the first death. The Garden is defined by what will not happen again, and the one death already behind them is named rather than erased.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing the surah's account of the God-conscious in their secure station. The audience were mostly people of modest means for whom imported silk was a distant luxury, brought up the incense road from further east. Commentators note the emphasis on facing one another and on security, both of which describe a social condition rather than a possession. No occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: A light silk, distinguished from the heavier fabric named beside it. The pairing of a fine and a thick material describes a full set of clothing rather than a single luxurious item.
A reciprocal form: each is turned toward the others. It describes seating and, through it, a company in which nobody is placed behind or below anyone else.
From the root behind faith and trust. It closes the list of pleasures with a state rather than an object, and it is the one item that no amount of provision can supply.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Where a person sat announced everything. In a Meccan assembly the arrangement of a gathering encoded rank precisely, and men knew without asking whether they were placed above or below someone. Silk arrived from far east of Arabia and was worn by very few. A description of people richly dressed and seated facing each other described both wealth and the removal of hierarchy at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The two fabrics named here appear together in only two places in the Quran. The other describes the Gardens of Eden and sits immediately before a parable about two men and their gardens. The word for facing one another is used across several descriptions of the Garden, always of seating, so how a gathering is arranged is repeatedly part of what is being described.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage builds its picture out of company and security rather than out of abundance alone, and the final line explains why that ordering works. What ends every gathering in this world is death, and its removal is stated as the last item rather than the first. Naming the first death rather than denying it also keeps the account honest: something happened, and it is not being unsaid.

crossReferences.why: Names the same two fabrics together, with reclining couches, in the other passage that pairs them.
Describes rancour removed from their breasts, brothers seated on couches facing one another.
Shows the same facing arrangement being used for conversation, with one of them turning to ask another.

studies.applyIt: At your next meal with more than one other person, arrange the seating so everyone can see everyone. It sounds trivial. This description of the Garden spends one of its four lines on how people are seated, which suggests the arrangement of a table is not a small part of what makes a gathering good.

studies.title: Made Easy In Your Tongue
studies.meaning: The whole preceding account is attributed to one source: a bounty from your Lord, and that is the great triumph. Then a statement about the text itself. We made it easy in your tongue so that they might take heed. Commentators read the easing as the language, the rhythm and the memorability together, all of which serve the same purpose. The surah then closes on two words facing each other. So watch and wait; they too are watching and waiting. Both sides are described as doing the same thing, and the sentence stops there.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, the final three ayat of a short surah. The community was small, the outcome undecided, and both sides in Mecca were genuinely waiting to see what would happen. Commentators note the surah ends without a resolution, which matches its situation. The claim about the language being made easy answers an audience for whom the recitation's memorability was a fact they could verify daily.

keyTerms.note: From a root for what remains over and above what is owed. Naming the whole preceding account as surplus removes it from the vocabulary of wages before the surah ends.
A verb for smoothing a path or making something manageable. The same verb runs through another surah as a refrain about this recitation being made easy to remember.
The participle of the verb that opened this surah's warning about the smoke. The chapter's first instruction and its last word come from that verb, so the frame closes on itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Memory was the medium. Poetry was carried in the head across generations, and a composition that could not be held was lost within a lifetime. Reciters were valued for retention as much as for delivery. A text described as made easy in the language of its hearers was making a claim they could test immediately, by finding out how much of it they had after one sitting.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for watching and waiting appears at both ends of this surah, as an instruction near its opening and again as its final word, describing the Prophet and his opponents doing exactly the same thing. This particular form of the verb occurs three times in the Quran, and two of the three are the first and last of this chapter.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage ends a surah of warnings on a note of shared suspense rather than of victory, which is unusually restrained. Both parties are described with the same participle, and no outcome is announced. It also grounds accessibility in the character of the revelation rather than in the effort of the reader. Being made easy is presented as a decision taken about the text, so difficulty is not the price of seriousness.

crossReferences.why: Repeats as a refrain that this recitation was made easy to remember, asking whether anyone will take heed.
Says it was made easy in your tongue so you may give good news with it and warn a contentious people.
Gives the only other use of this verb for watching, telling a prophet to watch and be patient.

studies.applyIt: Memorise two short ayat this week, any two, and recite them from memory once a day. Do not choose difficult ones. This surah closes by claiming the text was deliberately made easy to carry, and the only way to find out whether that is true about you is to try to carry a little of it.
